focus_area_title: Use I-PASS to Improve Handoff Communications
content_text_body:
Patient transitions or "handoffs" from one shift to the next or one department to the next are very prevalent in today's healthcare environments. During an average hospital stay, patients can interact with dozens of different healthcare professionals. Structured communication techniques are recommended to help prevent lapses in communication across these various individuals and teams. 
    
### Why is it important?

According to the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, handoffs have been tied to adverse events in clinical settings ranging from the emergency department to the intensive care unit. In a study published in the New England Journal of Medicine, when analyzing over 10,000 patient admissions across nine hospitals, researchers found that the medical error rate reduced by 23% and the adverse event rate by 30% after the I-PASS communication method was implemented amongst resident physicians.

**Over the course of two years, Starmer and her colleagues implemented the I-PASS bundle communication method across 9 pediatric hospitals in the U.S. and Canada and found very promising results in terms of reductions in safety issues. Below is a brief summary of I-PASS and the interventions the researchers implemented:**

- I-PASS is the basis for verbal and written communications between team members. The I-PASS mnemonic stands for:
>- Illness severity - brief identification of patient acuity (e.g., stable, unstable, watcher)  
>- Patient summary - brief reason for admission, events leading up to admission, hospital course, plan for hospitalization  
>- Action list - a "to-doâ€ list with specific elements to accomplish over the next shift by the team assuming care, timeframe for completion, level of priority, who is responsible.  If there is nothing to do, specify this  
>- Situation awareness and contingency plans - Situation awareness is knowing what is going on for members of the care team (status of patients, environmental factors, team members) and for each individual patient (status of disease process, progress towards goals for hospitalization). Contingency plans: With situation awareness in mind, provide team assuming care of the patient with specific instructions for how to handle anticipated problems. These often include "if/thenâ€ statements. Specify no contingencies expected for stable patients  
>- Synthesis by receiver - a brief re-statement of essential information in a cogent summary by the receiving team to ensure effective transfer of information and communication

- **Workshop or training on I-PASS**  
In addition to rolling out I-PASS to residents at these hospitals, researchers also had study participants go through a "bundle" of learning/education exercises to ensure I-PASS was practiced properly and sustained. One exercise was a 2-hour training/workshop on the I-PASS mnemonic, effective communication and teamwork techniques, and best practices for verbal and written handoffs.  

- **Handoff Simulations/Role-Playing**  
In addition to rolling out I-PASS to residents at these hospitals, researchers also had study participants go through a "bundleâ€ of learning/education exercises to ensure I-PASS was practiced properly and sustained. One of these exercises was a 1-hour interactive roleplay session to allow for the practicing of techniques learned in the resident workshop or online module.

- **Computer Module Exercise**  
In addition to rolling out I-PASS to residents at these hospitals, researchers also had study participants go through a "bundle" of learning/education exercises to ensure I-PASS was practiced properly and sustained. One exercise was a computer module for independent learning that reinforced the importance of effective communication to reduce safety errors, applying team training exercises to improve handoffs, and the importance of the content and sequence of effective handoffs.
